newsitem.title: USA: Los Angeles voters OK record $2.4 bln school bond.
newsitem.headline: Los Angeles voters OK record $2.4 bln school bond.

text.p: Voters in Los Angeles approved a record $2.4 billion bond measure to fund repairs and add classrooms at the Los Angeles Unified School District, according to semi-official election returns Wednesday.
No other school district in the country has ever approved a bond issue of this size, the measure's supporters said.
State and local officials hailed the election results.
"The Los Angeles vote demonstrates the strong commitment to education that is necessary for California's future," California state Treasurer Matt Fong said.
Erik Nasarenko, a spokesman for the bond campaign, said; "This is a victory for all of Los Angeles. These are basic brick and mortar repairs that every school needed."
The Los Angeles bond measure won the approval of over 70 percent of the voters, city election officials said. The measure required 66.67 percent approval for passage.
Municipal analysts said the election results were somewhat surprising given California's tough voter-approval requirements for local bond measures.
"For a major city to get two-thirds approval is pretty hard to do," Standard & Poor's Director David Hitchcock said.
The measure authorizes the Los Angeles Unified School District to issue $2.4 billion of general obligation bonds to fund improvements at more than 800 schools.

By law, expenditures can only be made for school buildings, classrooms and school grounds. No money from the sale of the bonds can be used for administrators' salaries. Each project will be monitored by an independent oversight committee, according to the school district.

Bond proceeds will be used to replace deteriorating roofing, heating, plumbing and electrical systems. The bonds will also fund earthquake reinforcement and asbestos removal, as well as class-size reduction programs.
The bonds would be repaid over a period not to exceed 25 years by a property tax levied on property owners in the school district, according to the proposition.
Hitchcock said S&P would review the credit implications of the huge bond measure. He said the rating agency plans to meet with district officials in May to discuss its issuance plans.

"Generally, the debt level (at the Los Angeles district) is relatively low," he said. He added that the bond measure's passage could be a credit positive for the district because it would provide a new source of tax revenue.
Last November, an identical Los Angeles Unified School District bond measure narrowly failed.
